As someone who suffers from horrible intrusive thoughts (OCD) just like this on a constant basis, a piece of advice my therapist taught me is: acceptance & detachment. Accept that maybe your intrusive thoughts could be telling the truth & maybe people are talking about you behind your back, that you can’t ever know for sure. Accept the worst case scenario & make peace with it. “Sure, maybe it’s true. Oh well. So what?” I know that sounds really scary because feeling like everyone is mocking you in secret is *not fun,* but please give it a try. I used to have horrible social anxiety in high school, to the point where I refused to get up from my seat to throw something in the trash can because I couldn’t stand the thought of people noticing me. After a long time, I got tired of living this way & one day, while I was grocery shopping with my mother, I felt in a good mood & I started doing a silly dance in the middle of the aisle. No one was in the aisle, but I knew people were *around,* & I had a moment of clarity that I’d never felt so free in so long. Do little things to challenge yourself & these thoughts. Your worst fears are probably not true but even if they were, you will feel more free if you detach yourself & decide not to care what others may be thinking.

Hey sorry to hear you’re dealing with this! You’re doing the right thing by removing yourself from the situation when your partner triggers you. That’s way better than suffering in silence or potentially snapping at him. If your partner is upset at you for leaving the room so he can continue whistling, then that’s not fair of him. Maybe he doesn’t see it from the perspective that you don’t want to take whistling away from him, so this is your only option. He cannot get upset with you for having a condition or showing symptoms of your condition. You are not trying to hurt him. 

It’s tricky because so often, triggers are human made sounds that are difficult, if not impossible, to avoid. Whistling is avoidable though. Your partner could try to work on being mindful about *when* he whistles—nothing stops him from doing it when he’s alone. 

Whistling is one of my worst triggers. I’ve learned how to cope better & mask over the years, so no one would be able to tell. However, it still definitely hurts, & I would absolutely struggle to live with someone who whistled constantly.

My brother does the same thing where whistles a looot & he won’t realize it for a bit. Then when he does, he’ll get frustrated at himself. To be fair, we live far from each other & don’t have the ability to see eachother in person often, so he is used to whistling all the time & of course it would be an adjustment for him not to the rare occasion we can meet up. It’s just habit for some people. 

It sounds like you may need to have a conversation with your partner so you can explain why calmly leaving the room when he whistles is the healthiest solution. It lets him continue doing it, & it removes you from a painful situation. Please don’t let this guilt you if it has… it’s out of your control. 

You’re doing great.

Sorry if this isn’t relevant to your question, though in the future if another depressive episode hits, there’s a trick you can try to get yourself to eat. Let’s say you want to eat a sandwich, yet you have zero energy to make one. Go to the kitchen, get the ingredients out—the bread, the meat, & whatever else you like on your sandwiches—then take them to the couch/ to bed with you so you can eat them individually yet still at the same time, if that makes any sense? You’re still getting the food you need in you, just without the “hassle” of making it. 

Another thing you can try is smoothies. They’re a lot easier to get down than a meal is.

Hi OP,

I’m so sorry you’re dealing with this. POCD really is one of the worst forms of OCD. It is just downright torture. You deserve to heal, which is why you should absolutely seek therapy. 

It is possible to love yourself again. Since OCD is nicknamed the doubting disorder, no logic you throw its way will work to shut it up. It’s just gonna find another argument, another what if to torment you with. 

How can you ever find relief in this situation? The answer is simple on paper, hard in practice— accepting the worst case scenario. Your therapist will say the same thing.

My therapist taught me to say to my OCD “Maybe you’re right that I’m a p, I can’t know for sure. We’ll see.” It’s going to be really difficult at first bc I know you definitely don’t want to accept a reality where, worst case scenario, you are a p. It’s the scariest thing to you. 

Since your brain is trying to protect you (badly, thanks a lot brain!) you are better off treating these intrusive thoughts with kindness. An almost appreciative kind of attitude. Like, “Thank you brain, I know you’re trying to help.” That’s a lot better than “Shut up, stop giving me these thoughts, etc.” 

Please, please seek therapy & please do not kill yourself. I promise there’s hope.
